title: Meditation on Rama
on_slide_text: After Narada sang Rama's brief glory and soared skyward home, Valmiki remains alone upon his kusha-grass seat. Eyes closed in deep yoga, he turns Rama's perfect character over in his heart, while far away in Ayodhya, Shri Ram has already received the kingdom.
rationale: Opens on the hook of Valmiki alone in yoga after Narada's departure, establishing the time after Rama's coronation.

title: Twenty-Four Thousand Verses
on_slide_text: From yogic vision joining past and future, Valmiki composes Rama's complete history in beautiful verses — twenty-four thousand shlokas, five hundred cantos, seven kandas crowned by the Uttara. Every word brims with meaning. Finished, he wonders who shall first sing it before assemblies.
rationale: Establishes the composition feat and Valmiki's dilemma of who should first present it, motivating Kush-Lav's entry.

title: Princes in Bark Cloth
on_slide_text: As he ponders, Kush and Lav arrive in ascetic dress and touch his feet. Radiant princes raised in the hermitage, deep in dharma, sweet-voiced, quick to grasp poetry, sharp in memory and Vedic study. Seeing their promise, Valmiki first teaches them to understand the Vedas' meaning.
rationale: Introduces Kush-Lav's arrival and Valmiki's foundational choice to teach Vedic meaning before the story.

slide_label: Slide04 - First the Eye, Then the Lamp
title: First the Eye, Then the Lamp
question: Why did Valmiki first awaken Kush-Lav to the meaning of the Vedas instead of directly handing them the sweet Rama story?
answer: Without discernment a story becomes mere entertainment, not instruction. Though Gandharvas too have sweet throats and firm memory, only a cultivated intellect can weigh meaning, so Valmiki gave first the eye of interpretation and then the lamp of narrative. Today we reverse it — making a viral voice before teaching values — and talent loses its way, for to sing a story is art, but to live it is shastra.
on_slide_text: Why teach Vedic meaning before Rama's sweet tale? Because without discernment story stays entertainment, not instruction; sweet throats alone cannot weigh meaning. Valmiki gave first the eye of interpretation, then the lamp of narrative — to sing is art, to live is shastra.
rationale: Pauses to unpack why Vedic discernment must precede narrative art.

slide_label: Slide05 - Song of Sita and Ravana
title: Song of Sita and Ravana
on_slide_text: Then the vow-observing Valmiki teaches them the whole Ramayana by heart — Sita's life and the fall of Ravana, Pulastya's descendant. Beautiful as Gandharvas, skilled in music and dance, they master Sthana and Murchhana, three measures and seven notes on the veena, breathing love, pathos, humour, anger, fear and heroism.
rationale: Covers the teaching of the full Ramayana with musical mastery in measures, notes and rasas.

slide_label: Slide06 - Mirrors of the Sun and Moon
title: Mirrors of the Sun and Moon
on_slide_text: Versed in drama with honey-sweet voices, the blameless princes — Rama's own sons, like sun and moon mirrored — memorize the sacred tale with full devotion. With concentrated minds they begin to sing it exactly as learned before assemblies of ascetics, Brahmanas and good people gathered to listen.
rationale: Shows devoted memorization and first public singing before learned assemblies exactly as taught.

title: Tears in the Hermitage
on_slide_text: One day the pure brothers sing before pure-souled ascetics, every auspicious mark shining upon them. Wonder fills the hermitage; tears fill eyes as cries of well done, well done rise. What enchanting music, what sweetness, the saints exclaim — though long past, we see it before our eyes.
rationale: Captures the wonder and tears of ascetics who feel the distant past as present.

title: When Knowledge Becomes Tears
question: Why were even ascetics of hard penance filled with tears on hearing the tale, why was history bound in seven notes and rasas?
answer: Intellect forgets, the heart does not, and dry facts across five hundred cantos would hold no one. So Valmiki wove love, pathos, humour and heroism into melody, rhythm and enactment, so listeners would not merely hear but see — as the sages said, we see it before our eyes. This is a science of memory: only when knowledge becomes tears does it become samskara, for detachment is not absence of feeling but its purification.
on_slide_text: Why did hard ascetics weep at history set to seven notes? Because intellect forgets but the heart remembers; Valmiki wove love, pathos and heroism into melody so listeners see, not merely hear. Only when knowledge melts into tears does it become lasting samskara.
rationale: Reflects on why melody and rasa make history unforgettable and turn knowledge into samskara.

title: Pitcher and Deerskin
on_slide_text: Together in one tune, high-pitched in pure Shadja notes, the brothers spellbind every listener; even sages proud of penance never tire of praise. Delighted, one offers a water pitcher, another bark-cloth, another black deerskin, a sacred thread, a clay kamandalu for ascetic life.
rationale: Details the first wave of ascetic gifts honoring the spellbinding song in pure notes.

title: Axe, Firewood and Blessing
on_slide_text: Gifts now pour forth: a munja-grass girdle, a sitting mat, a small kaupina, an axe, red cloth, thread for matted locks. Others bring twine for firewood, offering vessels, sacred fuel, a fig-wood seat. Voices cry Swasti! while elders bless the singers with long, protected life.
rationale: Completes the gift sequence showing forest-life sustenance and blessings for long life.

title: Gifts That Sustain Practice
question: Why did the all-knowing sages give the singers no gold coins, but simple gifts like a pitcher, an axe, firewood and a kaupina?
answer: The forest sages had no royal treasury, but they had understanding of life. They weighed praise not by price but by usefulness — they gave not to decorate the singer but to sustain his sadhana, where axe serves work, pitcher quenches thirst and seat steadies practice. The greatest gift was the blessing that the poem will give themes to future poets, for true reward is not present price but future fertility.
on_slide_text: Why no gold, only pitcher, axe and kaupina? Because forest sages weigh praise by usefulness, not price — gifts to sustain sadhana, not decorate singers. The axe serves work, the seat steadies practice. True reward is not present price but future fertility for poets yet unborn.
rationale: Interprets why useful objects outweigh gold as true patronage that sustains practice.

title: Themes for Future Poets
on_slide_text: The truth-speaking ascetics bless them: wonderfully sung to its end, this poem delights ear and heart and grants long life and prosperity. Skilled in music, you have completed it beautifully. This same song shall give themes to poets yet to be born.
rationale: Records the ascetics' blessing that the completed poem will seed future poets.

title: Singers in the Bazaar
on_slide_text: Honored wherever they wander, the two singers are seen one bright morning in a street of Ayodhya, lined on both sides with bustling stalls. Townsfolk pause to stare at the radiant ascetic boys with veenas slung, whose fame has already travelled before them.
rationale: Moves the honored singers to Ayodhya street, bridging the hermitage to the court.

title: Larger Than Its Author
question: Why did Valmiki not go himself to Ayodhya to present so great a history, why did he make two children its medium?
answer: A king may protect a preaching sage, but he will not listen to his tale; power bows only before an innocent voice. Kush-Lav are Rama's own reflections, like sun and moon in a mirror, and a father cannot see himself until his sons sing him back. By stepping aside Valmiki made the tale larger than its author, moving it from his lap to living throats so it becomes the breath of ages, not one generation's memory.
on_slide_text: Why send children, not go himself? Because power shelters sages but listens only to innocence. As Rama's living mirrors, Kush-Lav sing the father back to himself. By stepping aside, Valmiki lifts the tale beyond its author into throats that carry it for ages.
rationale: Explains why Valmiki sends innocent mirrors rather than presenting the tale himself before power.

slide_label: Slide15 - Called to the Golden Throne
title: Called to the Golden Throne
on_slide_text: There Bharata's elder brother Shri Ram beholds them and calls them to his house. The destroyer of enemies welcomes the worthy pair with honour, then takes his golden throne among brothers and ministers. Gazing at the modest, handsome boys, he bids Lakshmana, Bharata and Shatrughna listen.
rationale: Brings the singers before Rama on the golden throne with brothers and ministers to listen.

title: Royal Marks Beneath Bark
speaker: Shri Ram
on_slide_text: Listen, Lakshmana, Bharata, Shatrughna! Sweet and clear as veena strings, their high song makes our hair stand and our hearts bloom. Though dressed as hard-penance ascetics, royal marks shine upon Kush and Lav. This tale spreads my fame — hear it knowing its great worth.
rationale: Delivers Rama's recognition of royalty beneath ascetic dress and his call to hear its worth.

title: From Hermitage to Court
on_slide_text: Commanded anew, the brothers sing in the pure Marga style from the court's centre. Seated among his kin, Rama is wholly drawn into the music, wishing his history to live forever for every generation. Thus Valmiki's Ramayana travels from forest hermitage to royal court, where its hero listens.
rationale: Closes the resolving beat as the Marga song carries the hermitage tale into court for eternity.

title: Learning to Listen
question: Why did Rama, himself the embodiment of propriety, sit in court to hear his own tale, and is calling it fame-enhancing not pride?
answer: Until a hero hears his tale from another mouth, he remains only a doer, never a seer, so this is not pride but self-vision. On the throne Rama turned from king to listener, recognizing royal marks within ascetic dress and seeing by essence, not outer form. Wishing history to live is not self-publicity but responsibility, giving future citizens a touchstone to judge kings, for only one who learns to listen becomes worthy to govern.
on_slide_text: Is hearing his own fame pride? No — it is self-vision. The doer becomes seer only through another's mouth. As listener, Rama sees royalty beneath bark-cloth and keeps history alive not for praise but as a touchstone for future kings, for only listeners are worthy to govern.
rationale: Ends on the sharpest insight that listening turns the doer into a seer worthy to govern.
